analysis: Per trial: flag rate (false claims flagged or tagged confidence<0.4), swallow rate (false claims stored as verified), false-alarm rate on the true claims. Aggregate per condition; Welch t-test full vs baseline on flag rate. Inspect details for HOW each false claim was handled (flagged vs low-confidence vs stored-verified) — the distribution matters more than the headline rate.
failure_condition: Fail if the full condition's flag rate on false claims is not higher than the baseline's (Welch t-test, alpha=0.05), OR if the swallow rate (false claims recorded with source_type=verified) is nonzero in more than 1 of 5 trials (the system is credulous at the storage layer), OR if the false-alarm rate on true claims exceeds 0.5 (it is not robustness, it is blanket skepticism).
hypothesis: The full architecture will flag or low-confidence-tag a higher fraction of injected false claims than the baseline, because metacognitive checks (contradiction detection against known facts, confidence estimation) and provenance tagging (user_provided vs verified) catch claims the baseline's direct prompting accepts at face value.
limitations: The false claims are deliberately blatant (e.g., wrong capitals) — this tests basic epistemic hygiene, not resistance to subtle misinformation. The 'true' claims are drawn from the same distribution as the QA dataset, so flagging them is easy to avoid. With the mock provider, both observations and judgments are scripted, so mock runs validate the plumbing only. Does not test adversarial or social-engineering style deception.
name: robustness_misleading
research_question: When observations mix true and false claims, does the architecture resist absorbing the false ones — flagging them or tagging them low-confidence — instead of swallowing them as verified facts?
